title: Escaped Markup: Preventing Verdict Spoofing in Structured Multimodal LLM Judges

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution aims to characterize a new attack surface created by structured output formats in multimodal LLM judges. Paper [13] introduces the Constrained Decoding Attack (CDA), which targets structured output APIs in LLMs, identifying vulnerabilities in grammar-guided decoding. This aligns with the purpose of exposing structured output vulnerabilities, albeit in a slightly different context. Paper [9] also discusses novel security risks in LLM-as-a-Judge systems, including adversarial manipulation, but does not specifically focus on structured output formats. Paper [3] investigates universal adversarial attacks on LLM judges but does not address structured output formats. Thus, paper [13] substantively covers the purpose.

### Mechanism
The contribution uses a format-spoofing attack that appends a suffix to the dispreferred candidate, injecting reserved markers to construct a fake output structure that the judge pattern-completes. Paper [13] introduces CDA, which exploits grammar-guided decoding vulnerabilities in structured output APIs, relying on structural marker collisions. This is substantively equivalent to the format-spoofing mechanism described in the contribution. Paper [6] discusses spoofing attacks via false data injections but focuses on cyber-physical systems, not structured output formats in LLMs. Paper [16] studies spoofing attacks on Kalman filters, which is unrelated to the mechanism here. Thus, paper [13] covers the mechanism.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates attack success rates using VL-RewardBench with Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, measuring conditional attack success rate (ASRcond). Paper [13] evaluates CDA using structured output APIs but does not use VL-RewardBench or measure ASRcond. Paper [4] evaluates prompt injection attacks on LLM-as-a-Judge systems using success rates but does not use the same evaluation design. Paper [9] provides a comprehensive SoK on LLM-as-a-Judge security but does not introduce a specific evaluation design. No prior paper uses the same evaluation design (VL-RewardBench with ASRcond), so evaluation is uncovered.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of AI alignment and adversarial attacks on multimodal LLM-as-a-Judge systems. Paper [9] explicitly addresses security risks in LLM-as-a-Judge systems, covering adversarial manipulation and reliability concerns. Paper [4] evaluates prompt injection attacks on LLM-as-a-Judge systems across multiple models and tasks, which falls within the same domain. Paper [3] investigates adversarial attacks on LLM judges, also within the same domain. Thus, the domain is covered by multiple prior papers.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to provide a practical training-free defense that neutralizes injected markers in prompt injection attacks. None of the prior papers explicitly propose a training-free defense targeting injected markers. Papers like [3] (PromptArmor) and [10] (Polymorphic Prompt Assembling) propose defenses against prompt injection attacks, but they rely on mechanisms like prompting an LLM or assembling polymorphic prompts, which are not training-free. Therefore, no prior paper shares the same purpose.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves reserved-sequence sanitization through sequential preprocessing steps: tag stripping, boxed removal, verdict redaction, quality-assertion redaction, and blank-line cleanup. Papers [7] (Data Sanitization), [13] (Text Preprocessing Pipeline), [15] (Data Cleansing), and [21] (Validating and Sanitizing User Input) describe sanitization or preprocessing pipelines, but none specifically address reserved-sequence sanitization for prompt injection markers. Paper [14] (Regex Denial of Service) discusses regex-based sanitization, which overlaps with the boxed removal step, but the broader mechanism (reserved-sequence sanitization) is not covered. Thus, no prior paper fully matches the mechanism.

### Evaluation
The evaluation validates the defense as a training-free preprocessing pipeline against No Defense and Spotlighting baselines. Paper [20] (Spotlighting) uses Spotlighting as a defense mechanism and evaluates it against indirect prompt injection attacks, which matches the evaluation design of comparing defenses against prompt injection attacks. Therefore, the evaluation facet is covered.

### Domain
The domain is prompt-injection defense for structured LLM judges. Papers [3] (PromptArmor), [10] (Polymorphic Prompt Assembling), and [20] (Spotlighting) all address prompt injection defenses for LLMs, which is the same general application area. While the contribution targets structured LLM judges specifically, this is a narrower instance within the broader domain of prompt injection defense, making the domain covered.
